newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda set to launch programme to end poverty.
newsitem.headline: Uganda set to launch programme to end poverty.

text.p: Uganda will launch a massive campaign to eradicate poverty and bolster economic growth with the 1997/98 state budget to be presented to parliament on Thursday, leading government officials said on Tuesday.

That means taxes will be further streamlined, luxuries such as cabinet ministers travelling first class on foreign trips will end and huge salary increases for government employees will not be considered, officials said.

They added the government would aim to spend less than its revenues and would quicken the pace for privatisation of state utilities and the opening of the Kampala bourse as new avenues for cash to finance its "people-centred" programmes.

The government's ambitions are strengthened by a World Bank decision to approve a reduction in external debt for Uganda, $338 million of the total $3.4 billion in April 1998, under a programme for highly indebted poor countries.
That means a smaller burden in debt servicing.
"Beginning with the development budget this year, we shall focus on eradication of poverty more than we've ever done," said Planning and Economic Development Minister Richard Kaijuka.
Kaijuka told Reuters ahead of the budget speech that areas of government attention were education, health and infrastructure.

President Yoweri Museveni has made UPE (Universal Primary Education) -- a major campaign pledge in presidential elections he won in 1995 -- a preoccupation in recent months. It guarantees free primary education for four children per family.
UPE allocation in the budget is 45 billion shillings ($42 million) out of 840 billion in forecast revenues for 1997/98.

Kaijuka said Uganda's "poverty-focused" budget would make provisions for repair of roads, water sanitation and developing human capacity. It would also guarantee distribution of high yield seeds across the fertile country to avert food shortages.
"Cabinet ministers have actually called for cuts in government spending. Luxuries and areas of less priority will have to be dropped," Kaijuka told Reuters in an interview.

Treasury Permanent Secretary Emmanuel Tumusiime Mutebile last month told parliament the 1997/98 budget would be the most stringent in recent years as the reformist Museveni turns his energies to the lives of ordinary Ugandans.
The government will put 28 billion shillings in financing local government elections to get ordinary folk involved in planning their areas, a government official said.

Museveni has rejected planned annual allowances of $180,000 and a salary increase to 4.5 million shillings per month, believed to be double his current salary, for himself, according to government officials.

Vice-President Specioza Wandira Kazibwe has rejected proposals for $135,000 in family allowances and clothes. She has also refused a salary increase to 3.5 million shillings per month from an unspecified figure, government officials said.
Museveni has reduced his own entourage and cut the number of state cars ministers are allowed to one from two.
Uganda's real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at around 7.0 percent in 1996/97 from 8.2 percent in 1995/96 and 10 percent in 1994/95. Inflation is in the single-digit zone.
